steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Monitor eGFR and serum potassium within 1–2 weeks of initiating or titrating RAAS inhibitors.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Use statins with caution in active hepatic disease; monitor baseline ALT/AST.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and statins are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).
special_populations.elderly: Avoid overtreatment; monitor for orthostatic hypotension and fall risk.

style_3_monograph.summary: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), previously known as Wegener's granulomatosis, is a rare disease. It is a type of vasculitis , or inflammation of the blood vessels. The inflammation limits the flow of blood to important organs, causing damage. It can affect any organ, but it mainly affects the sinuses, nose, trachea (windpipe), lungs, and kidneys. The cause of GPA is unknown. It can affect people at any age. Men and women are equally affected. It is more common in whites. Symptoms may include joint pain, weakness, tiredness, and cold symptoms such as a runny nose that doesn't get better. Doctors use blood tests, chest X-rays, and biopsies to diagnose GPA and rule out other causes of the symptoms. Early treatment is important. Most people improve with medicines to slow or stop the inflammation.
style_3_monograph.treatment: Because of the potentially serious nature of GPA, you may be hospitalized. Once the diagnosis is made, you will probably be treated with high doses of glucocorticoids (such as prednisone). These are given through the vein for 3 to 5 days at the beginning of treatment. Prednisone is given along with other medicines that slow down the immune response. For milder disease other medicines that slow down the immune response such as methotrexate or azathioprine may be used. Common medicines for vasculitis include: Rituximab (Rituxan) Cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan) Methotrexate Azathioprine (Imuran) These medicines are effective in severe disease, but they may cause serious side effects. Most people with GPA are treated with ongoing medicines to prevent relapse for at least 12 to 24 months. Talk to your health care provider about your treatment plan. Other medicines used for GPA include: Medicines to prevent bone loss caused by prednisone Folic acid or folinic acid, if you are taking methotrexate Antibiotics to prevent lung infections
